description: Per-capita yearly means by country (carbon kg CO2e incl. land use, water withdrawals L, agricultural land m²·yr (world average, since territorial land misattributes food exporters), electricity demand kWh). The cohort model converts means to lognormal medians with median = mean·exp(−σ²/2). US states scale the US carbon mean by their production-based EIA ratio, clamped to [stateRatioMin, stateRatioMax].

usStates.note: EIA figures are production-based (power plants, refineries and industry that serve other states), so they spread far wider (MA 0.57×, WY 6.5× the US) than what residents consume; the ratio is clamped to 0.8–1.25× so a state baseline stays a plausible personal footprint.

citation.title: US EIA, Energy-related CO2 emissions by state, Table 4: per capita (2022)

sigmas.note: Carbon σ is narrower than WIR's ownership-based inequality (which attributes investment emissions to owners): a personal consumption footprint at σ 0.45 has its 10th–90th percentiles at 0.56×–1.78× the median (US ≈ 9–28 t).

citation.title: Chancel, Piketty et al., World Inequality Report 2022 (carbon inequality within countries); lognormal σ derived

plantBasedFoodShares.note: Share of the average diet's food footprint left on a diet without animal products. Poore & Nemecek find dropping animal products cuts food's GHG emissions by 49%, land use by 76% and freshwater withdrawals by 19%; carbon also matches Scarborough et al.'s vegan-to-meat-eater ratio (0.51).

citation.title: Poore & Nemecek (2018), Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers, Science 360:987

mealCarbon.note: kg CO2e a meal adds over a plant-based meal when meat (poultry, fish) or dairy is an important component. Meat: medium meat-eaters (5.63 kg CO2e/day, about one meat meal a day) minus vegetarians (3.81). Dairy: vegetarians minus vegans (2.89), spread over about two dairy meals a day. Only the meat-to-dairy ratio enters the modifier.

citation.title: Scarborough et al. (2014), Dietary greenhouse gas emissions of meat-eaters, fish-eaters, vegetarians and vegans in the UK, Climatic Change 125:179

averageMealsPerWeek.note: The average diet the per-capita food share stands for: US loss-adjusted availability of about 140 g of meat, poultry and fish a day (nine ~110 g portions a week) and about 1.5 cup-equivalents of dairy a day (about ten dairy-centred meals a week).

citation.title: USDA Economic Research Service, Food Availability (Per Capita) Data System: loss-adjusted food availability

clothingPurchases.note: Americans bought 64 garments and 7.5 pairs of shoes per person in 2013. baseShare is the part of clothing carbon that does not scale with new garments (footwear, second-hand finds, upkeep); 7.5 pairs at ~14 kg CO2e a pair (Cheah et al. 2013) is about a seventh.

citation.title: American Apparel & Footwear Association, ApparelStats 2014 (64 garments per person in 2013)

typicalFloorAreaM2.note: Average total floor area per housing unit, RECS 2020 table HC10.9: single-family detached 2,264 ft², single-family attached 1,615 ft², apartments 926 ft² (unit-weighted 2–4 and 5+ unit buildings). Dorm rooms (250 ft²) are an assumption; RECS does not survey them.

citation.title: U.S. EIA, Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) 2020, Table HC10.9: Average square footage of U.S. homes

spaceConditioningShare.note: Space heating and air conditioning were 52% of household energy in 2020; that part scales with floor area against a typical home of the same type, the rest (water heating, appliances, lighting) does not.

citation.title: U.S. EIA, Energy Explained: Use of energy in homes (RECS 2020)
Ivanova et al. (2016), Environmental Impact Assessment of Household Consumption, J. Ind. Ecol. 20:526
Underwood & Zahran (2015), The carbon implications of declining household scale, Ecological Economics 116:182

homeTypeModifiers.note: Household electricity use by housing type relative to the U.S. household average; dorms are taken as below apartments (shared, small, no major appliances).

citation.title: U.S. EIA, Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) 2020: household electricity consumption by housing type

heatingModifiers.note: Household electricity use by main space-heating fuel relative to the U.S. household average: electrically heated homes draw more, fuel-heated homes less. A home with several sources averages theirs evenly.

citation.title: U.S. EIA, Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) 2020: household electricity consumption by main space-heating fuel

heatingCarbonModifiers.note: Home-energy carbon by space-heating source relative to the U.S. household average, for the same heat delivered. RECS 2020 CE4.1: the average home's site energy (electricity 36.0, natural gas 34.3, propane 3.2, fuel oil 3.2 million Btu) is 5.95 t CO2e at the eGRID2023 U.S. grid (349.7 g/kWh) and ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager fuel factors (natural gas 53.11, propane 61.95, No. 2 fuel oil 74.2, district steam or hot water 66.40 kg CO2e per million Btu, Aug 2025 technical reference); space heating is 2.02 t of it (34%) and delivers about 28.5 million Btu of heat (furnaces 80%, oil 83%, electric heat 1.32 with heat pumps, 40% of electrically heated homes in RECS HC6.1, at a seasonal COP of 2.5). Each source keeps the rest and supplies that heat at its own carbon per unit of heat: gas 66, district 66, oil 89, resistance 102.5, heat pump 41 kg CO2e per million Btu; no heating keeps only the rest. Combustion and power-plant emissions only (no upstream methane). A home with several sources averages theirs evenly.

citation.title: U.S. EIA, Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) 2020, Table CE4.1: Annual household site end-use consumption by fuel (with US EPA eGRID2023 and ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager Greenhouse Gas Emissions Technical Reference, Aug 2025)
Ivanova et al. (2016), Environmental Impact Assessment of Household Consumption, J. Ind. Ecol. 20:526
